Chedorlaomer
ked-or-lā-ō'mer
n. (the king of Elam who headed the confederacy of four kings that sacked Sodom and carried Lot away, and whom Abram overthrew with three hundred and eighteen trained servants)
From Hebrew Kedorla'omer, an Elamite name generally analysed as servant of Lagamar, an Elamite deity. He is the first named overlord in Scripture and the first man in the Bible to receive tribute from other kings.

Biblical Definition

Chedorlaomer king of Elam is the head of the first war narrated in the Bible. Four eastern kings held the cities of the plain in vassalage: “Twelve years they served Chedorlaomer, and in the thirteenth year they rebelled” (Gen 14:4). His punitive campaign in the fourteenth year is described as a sweep down the whole eastern side of the Jordan rift, smiting Rephaims, Zuzims, Emims and Horites before turning back to the five rebel cities. The lineup is stated formally: “With Chedorlaomer the king of Elam, and with Tidal king of nations, and Amraphel king of Shinar, and Arioch king of Ellasar; four kings with five” (Gen 14:9). Sodom and Gomorrah fell, the slime pits swallowed the fleeing armies, and the raiders took the goods and the people — including Lot. Then a private man with a household militia overtook an imperial coalition: Abram armed his trained servants, three hundred and eighteen of them, pursued to Dan, divided himself against them by night, and brought back all the goods and all the people. Melchizedek met him returning “from the slaughter of Chedorlaomer, and of the kings that were with him” (Gen 14:17), and blessed him from the most high God, possessor of heaven and earth. The whole later theology of tithe and priesthood in Hebrews 7 hangs on that meeting, and the meeting happened because Chedorlaomer took the wrong nephew.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) has no article for Chedorlaomer; in sacred history he is the king of Elam who held the cities of the plain in subjection and was defeated by Abram.

expand to see more

CHEDORLAOMER, n. A king of Elam in the days of Abram the Hebrew.

The cities of the plain served him twelve years, and in the thirteenth they rebelled.

He came with three confederate kings and smote the nations on both sides of the Jordan.

He spoiled Sodom and Gomorrah and carried away Lot, Abram's brother's son.

Abram pursued him with three hundred and eighteen trained servants and recovered all.

Key Scripture

Gen 14:4 — "Twelve years they served Chedorlaomer, and in the thirteenth year they rebelled."

Gen 14:5 — "And in the fourteenth year came Chedorlaomer, and the kings that were with him, and smote the Rephaims in Ashteroth Karnaim, and the Zuzims in Ham, and the Emims in Shaveh Kiriathaim,"

Gen 14:9 — "With Chedorlaomer the king of Elam, and with Tidal king of nations, and Amraphel king of Shinar, and Arioch king of Ellasar; four kings with five."

Gen 14:17 — "And the king of Sodom went out to meet him after his return from the slaughter of Chedorlaomer, and of the kings that were with him, at the valley of Shaveh, which is the king's dale."

Modern Corruption

Genesis 14 is routinely treated as a late legendary insertion because it names kings the modern historian cannot securely identify. The chapter reads as sober annals, and the dictionary receives it as history, not as saga.

expand to see more

The standard academic handling of this chapter is to call it an isolated fragment of uncertain date, its four kings unidentifiable and its details therefore suspect — legendary material shaped to glorify Abram. That verdict rests on an assumption, not a finding: that a narrative naming kings we cannot yet cross-reference is thereby doubtful. Genesis 14 is written in the manner of a campaign record. It gives regnal arithmetic, a route, the peoples smitten at each stage, the tactics of the pursuit, the size of Abram's force to the man, and the terms of the settlement afterward. Silence in the surviving tablets of the second millennium is not evidence; the record of that world is fragmentary in the extreme, and it has repeatedly filled in later.

The dictionary receives Moses' account as what it presents itself to be. The New Testament rests real doctrine on the chapter's historicity: Hebrews argues the superiority of Christ's priesthood from Melchizedek meeting a real Abraham returning from a real slaughter of real kings, and paying him a real tenth — “unto whom even the patriarch Abraham gave the tenth of the spoils” (Heb 7:4). Dissolve Chedorlaomer into legend and the argument of Hebrews 7 has nothing under it. That is the ordinary pattern: the historical-critical solvent is never applied to the history alone.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Kedorla'omer (H3540), Chedorlaomer; 'Elam (H5867), Elam; chaniyk (H2593), trained servant, retainer; rekush (H7399), goods, substance; ma'aser (H4643), tithe, tenth part.

expand to see more

Hebrew Kedorla'omer (H3540) — Chedorlaomer; king of Elam and head of the four.

Hebrew 'Elam (H5867) — Elam; the kingdom east of Babylonia.

Hebrew chaniyk (H2593) — trained servant; the three hundred and eighteen of Abram's house.

Hebrew rekush (H7399) — goods, substance; the plunder recovered entire.

Hebrew ma'aser (H4643) — tithe; what Abram gave Melchizedek of the spoil.

Usage

"“Twelve years they served Chedorlaomer” — the first tribute in Scripture."

"“Four kings with five” — the ledger of the Bible's first war."

"“From the slaughter of Chedorlaomer” — the campaign that occasioned Melchizedek's blessing."
